title: Detecting misleading statistical diagrams
summary: Audit axes, spacing, class widths, symbols and selected ranges before accepting a visual comparison.
objectives: Identify common construction choices that exaggerate or conceal differences.
Quantify the effect of a truncated axis or distorted scale.
Describe how to redraw a diagram fairly.

blocks.text: The diagram shows a truncated vertical axis: it starts at 94 instead of 0. Such an axis is not automatically invalid, but it can exaggerate small differences if the break is unclear. Time points must be spaced according to their actual intervals. Labels, units and a consistent scale allow the reader to judge what is shown.

sections.title: Check whether visual size matches data

blocks.text: In a histogram with unequal class widths, frequency must be represented by area, so height is frequency density. Pictograms using two-dimensional pictures must control area: doubling both height and width multiplies area by four, not two.

A selectively chosen start date can reverse the impression of a longer trend. Compare the displayed window with the claim being made, check whether categories are omitted, and distinguish absolute changes from percentage changes. A fair redesign should retain relevant context and use proportional visual encoding.

sections.title: Worked example: quantify a truncated axis

prompt.text: In the diagram, sales of 98 and 102 thousand are drawn from a baseline of 94. Compare their visible heights with the actual change.

content.text: Visible heights are measured from the baseline.
The second bar looks twice as tall as the first.
The actual increase is 4 thousand out of 98 thousand.

sections.verification_note: Drawn from 0, the bars would be 98 and 102 units tall, almost the same height, which matches the small 4.1% increase.

sections.title: Worked example: correct an unequal-width histogram

prompt.text: Classes of widths 5 and 10 both have frequency 20. Find the heights to draw.

content.text: Height is frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
Draw the first bar 4 units high and the second 2 units high.

sections.verification_note: Both bars then have area 5 × 4 = 10 × 2 = 20, so equal frequencies get equal areas, not equal heights.

prompt.text: On a bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 45, two bars show the values 50 and 55. How many times as tall as the first bar does the second bar look?

feedback.text: Visible heights are 50 − 45 = 5 and 55 − 45 = 10, so the second bar looks 2 times as tall, although 55 is only 10% more than 50.

blocks.text: Check where the vertical axis starts, whether time points are evenly spaced for equal intervals, whether histogram bars use frequency density, and whether pictures change in area as well as height.
Quantify the distortion, for example by comparing visible heights with the actual percentage change, and describe a fair redesign.
